body.x: In a busy restaurant, much of a server's shift goes to carrying plates and bowls between the kitchen and the tables. When labor costs rise and staff are hard to find, that repetitive carrying work competes with time that could go to customers and cooking.

Creambot Co., Ltd., a service robot company based in Seo-gu, Incheon, is built around that problem. Led by CEO Chanyoung Kim, the company will take part in FIX 2026 through the 15th Daegu International Robot Industry Expo (ROBEX 2026), where it plans to show AI-powered service robots including serving, cleaning and logistics models.

Creambot says it supplies AI-based service robots such as serving robots, cleaning robots and hotel delivery and logistics robots, with installation and maintenance services tailored to each customer's operating environment. It serves the food service, hospitality, healthcare and commercial sectors, and the company says its aim is to improve operating efficiency and ease the burden of staffing. It says it has built smart service environments for customers through a nationwide sales and service network.

According to the company, its biggest difference is field-oriented service capability: introducing robots to fit a customer's actual operating environment and supporting them from installation through maintenance. Creambot says it goes beyond supplying robots by offering a tailored solution that takes the space and operating characteristics of each store or facility into account. It adds that a lineup spanning serving, cleaning and hotel delivery and logistics robots lets customers automate a range of tasks with one supplier.

Creambot is exhibiting three products. The serving robot T10 carries food and goods using autonomous driving technology. The company says it has obstacle recognition and avoidance and automatic charging, and that it can be used in restaurants, cafes, hotels and hospitals. The logistics robot S100 is an industrial autonomous robot that moves bulk materials along designated routes in factories, distribution centers and hospitals, which the company says reduces workers' travel and optimizes the flow of goods. The cleaning robot C40 cleans floor dust and dirt with suction, wet mopping, obstacle avoidance and automatic charging, and is used in offices, hospitals, hotels and shopping malls, according to Creambot.

The company describes its restaurant robots as a way to reduce staffing pressure. In its words, the serving robot automates repetitive work such as carrying food and dishes so that employees can concentrate on serving customers and cooking, which it says raises store efficiency and lowers staffing costs and burden.

Creambot also says it is developing an AI-based remote medical service system to support non-face-to-face consultations, in response to the growing adoption of digital healthcare at medical institutions. It says it is refining the technology so the robots can handle consultation guidance, calling medical staff and delivering medicines and medical supplies in remote care settings that connect doctors and patients.

Its target customers, the company says, are food service businesses facing staff shortages and labor costs, such as restaurants, large franchise outlets and food courts, where serving and carrying tasks recur. Creambot is also widening its customer range to lodging facilities such as hotels and resorts, hospitals and medical institutions, and large commercial facilities.

Creambot has no exports at present. The company lists the U.S., Japan, Singapore, Vietnam and Thailand as the markets it wants to enter, and it plans to push expansion mainly in Japan and Southeast Asia. It says rising labor costs and labor shortages in food service are increasing demand for service robots in these markets, and that Japan and Singapore show strong demand for robot-based efficiency because of aging populations and shortages of service workers.

The company's main difficulty is service. Because installation, maintenance and after-sales care matter as much as the sale of a serving robot, building a local service network overseas is hard. Creambot says it hopes to secure a stable base for overseas entry through support in finding overseas buyers and local partners and in handling export procedures for each country.

Its plan is to expand exports in earnest and to find local buyers and distribution and sales partners in the U.S., Japan and Southeast Asia. The company intends to attend overseas exhibitions and business meetings to win new accounts, and to build a supply system suited to each local market. It also plans to keep adding to its service robot lineup, including cleaning robots and hotel delivery and logistics robots, to extend into food service, hotels and lodging, medical institutions and commercial facilities. Over the medium to long term, Creambot says it wants to refine smart service solutions that combine AI and robotics and to build a sales, installation and maintenance network with overseas partners.

Creambot says its reasons for exhibiting are to widen contact with robot industry figures and potential customers in Korea and abroad, to promote the competitiveness of its serving robots and find new customers and buyers in food service, hospitality and commercial facilities, and to learn about the latest technology and industry trends. It also wants to build networks and look for cooperation with related companies and institutions, and to strengthen its brand awareness and market competitiveness as a service robot company.

FIX 2026 is the third edition of a future-industry exhibition in Daegu that combines and links innovative technologies in future mobility, robotics, AI and ICT, and startups. It takes place from Wednesday, Oct. 21, to Saturday, Oct. 24, at EXCO. Organized around the theme "AI, Beyond Tech into Reality," it offers AI-based technology exhibitions, conferences and lectures by experts from Korea and abroad, and networking programs where visitors can follow industry trends and core technologies.
